headline: When simple baselines are actually trained and scored, the rolling-origin by-Congress split (S3: train on 108..c-2, validate on c-1, refit on 108..c-1, test on c) does its job: validation picks near-best models and predicts Task 1 test levels. It works best with streaming same-Congress history, recency weighting, Task 2 selection averaged over several validation Congresses, and Congress 118 held back as a locked final test. A single test Congress (S1a/S1b) is too small to confirm real model differences, and the random split inflates Recall@20 by about 0.075.
overview:
Sections A-C checked the *preconditions* of a temporal split. This section checks the *consequence*. Each candidate split is used to train and score transparent baselines. Task 1 has count heuristics (`popularity`, `party+pop`, `sponsor_hist`), a 2-hop random-walk graph score (`rw2hop`, a fixed-weight version of SGC/LightGCN propagation) and a learned transductive embedding (`svd`). Task 2 has smoothed rates (`chamber_maj`, `eb_rate`, `eb_rate_t0safe`). The questions are whether validation picks the right model, whether test sets can resolve paired differences, whether validation predicts the test *level*, and which protocol choices cost or gain accuracy. All uncertainty comes from a 500-resample cluster bootstrap by sponsor (bills of the same sponsor are resampled together). The minimum detectable effect (MDE) is fixed at 0.01 Recall@20 / 0.01 AUROC. The tally is 15 PASS, 3 FAIL and 12 INFO.

**What the data shows.** (1) Under S3, validation choices transfer. Mean selection regret is 0.0028 Recall@20 for `sponsor_hist`, 0.0002 for `rw2hop`, 0.0007 for `svd`, and 0.0045 AUROC for the at-introduction Task 2 family (D11, D21, D23, D12b). Task 1 val-test gaps are within bootstrap noise (D1, D20, D22). (2) Paired model differences are stable on average but not in every single Congress. For the deployable Task 2 pair `eb_rate_t0safe - chamber_maj` (mean +0.020 AUROC), 3 of 7 single test Congresses (43%) fail to confirm the direction. That is why every single-test-Congress split fails D9. (3) Among valid temporal splits, protocol choices move scores more than the choice between S2 and S3 (the random split's +0.075 optimism is a split choice and is larger than every protocol effect except refitting). Streaming same-Congress history adds +0.037 Recall@20 in 7/7 folds. Refitting on train+val adds about +0.06. Recency weighting removes the advantage a 3-Congress sliding window has over the expanding window (-0.012 -> -0.0008). Upweighting regime-matched Congresses adds nothing beyond recency. (4) Two sources of optimism are large. The random split adds +0.075 Recall@20 (about 29% of the temporal level of 0.259). If Task 2 is scored at introduction, a policy area that usually does not exist yet adds +0.10 AUROC, about 45% of `eb_rate`'s discrimination above chance (0.10 of 0.22).

**What we infer.** The defensible protocol is the notebook's `D_FINAL_PROTOCOL`. Develop on S3(+stream) rolling folds 112-117, report once on locked Congress 118, and treat 119 as the prospective test. Reserving 118 is affordable: the maximum paired miss risk rises from 0.033 to 0.115, still under the 0.20 bar (D27). One cost: on the 6 development folds, the at-introduction Task 2 family's selection regret rises to 0.0053 AUROC, just above the 0.005 tolerance (it passes only because no fold is significant), so Task 2 hyperparameters should be chosen on the mean of several validation Congresses (D17: regret 0.0019), not on c-1 alone. Report Task 2 *levels* per Congress with their spread, never as one number. They move by more than sampling noise from Congress to Congress (D3/D4, D2b), and a precise average level would need about 13 Congresses (D15).

**Statistical caveats.** The 7 rolling folds are not independent: consecutive folds share almost all training Congresses, and each test Congress is the next fold's validation Congress. Fold counts ("2 of 7 significant") and sign tests are therefore descriptive, not exact. 18 checks carry a verdict (15 PASS, 3 FAIL; the 12 INFO items are descriptive, not tests), each at the 5% level with no multiplicity correction, so one verdict could flip by chance. Borderline verdicts, such as D12's mean regret of 0.0078 resting on a single fold, deserve less weight than consistent 7/7 patterns. The baselines are stand-ins: the SVD is the only learned model, and its edge over unweighted `sponsor_hist` (+0.021) is confounded with recency weighting (recency alone adds +0.021 to `sponsor_hist`, D26), so the data do not show that low-rank learning beats recency-weighted counts. GNN-specific failure modes, such as overfitting via message passing, are also only approximated. The MDE of 0.01 is a stated convention, not something estimated from the data.

D-c112-txt.interpretation: The engine covers 1,452 legislators, 128,791 law-capable bills in Congresses 108-118 and 110,802 uncensored advancement labels. It also fixes how often the policy area is hidden in the at-introduction Task 2 baseline: 86% of 119th bills that were 7 days old or less at the snapshot had no policy area yet (14% at 8-30 days).
D-c112-txt.caveats: The 86% comes from only 56 fresh bills in an in-progress Congress, and it is applied to every historical Congress. CRS assignment lag may have changed over time, so `eb_rate_t0safe` approximates at-introduction information rather than reproducing it exactly.

D-c113-txt.interpretation: This is the master table of mean test scores per split. It covers 60 units and 2,160 result rows, with no subsampling. On Task 1 Recall@20 at t0=0, the history-based scores (`sponsor_hist`, `rw2hop`) beat `party+pop` and `popularity` under every split. Plain by-Congress splits give 0.22-0.27 (S1pool 0.222, S1b 0.244, S3 0.259, S2 0.272). Streaming variants, which also add same-Congress history up to t0, are about 0.04-0.05 higher (S3+stream 0.296, S1b+stream 0.297). The two splits that *train* on same-Congress bills score higher still: S4 0.310 (Congresses 116-118, test = last 20% of bills) and the leaky random split S5 0.332. On Task 2, `eb_rate` AUROC is 0.69-0.72 on by-Congress splits but only 0.55-0.63 for the at-introduction version `eb_rate_t0safe`. Only 0.08% of Task 1 positives fall outside the point-in-time candidate pool (median pool size 434); the separate rerun in D18 confirms that the pool definition moves Recall@20 by only about +0.002.
D-c113-txt.caveats: Splits evaluate different Congresses and different numbers of folds, so columns are not paired comparisons; in particular S4 (3 Congresses, late bills only) is not paired with S3+stream (7 Congresses, all bills). Single-Congress columns (S1a = 117, S1b = 118) partly reflect how hard that Congress is. The S4 Task 2 AP lift of 3.89 rests on about 596 test bills per fold and should not be read as a real gain.

D-c115-txt.interpretation: On Task 1, validation predicts the test level. Under S3 the mean |test - val| for `sponsor_hist` is 0.011 Recall@20, and every per-fold gap (from -0.018 to +0.007) is inside its paired 95% half-width (0.024-0.029). D1 and D20 pass for every split except S1pool, whose val Congress 116 overstates its pooled 117+118 test by 0.032 (a 12% relative gap, 0.1196 in the calibration table, versus 0.038 expected from noise). On Task 2, `eb_rate` gaps are larger: 3 of 7 S3 folds (43%) are significant, for example +0.055 at c=112 and -0.055 at c=116. D2b fails for the at-introduction model under all multi-fold splits (S2, S3, S3+stream, S4) and under both single-fold splits tested on 118 (S1b, S1b+stream): its AUROC level moves between consecutive Congresses by more than noise.
D-c115-txt.caveats: D2b concerns calibration and level reporting, not model selection. Selection is tested directly in D12/D12b and passes. The chi-square treats folds as independent, but consecutive folds share Congresses. The single-fold splits pass D1 partly because a test with one degree of freedom has little power.

D-c115-o1.interpretation: The chart shows val and test Recall@20 (`sponsor_hist`) side by side for each split or fold. For the by-Congress splits the two dots nearly overlap (S1a 0.254 vs 0.262; S2 c=117 0.269 vs 0.274), so the validation Congress is a good proxy for the test level. In S4, test is above val in all three Congresses (for example 0.276 vs 0.319 in 118), with intervals about twice as wide. S5 sits clearly higher (val 0.323, test 0.332) than any plain by-Congress test score.
D-c115-o1.caveats: One plausible reason S4 test beats S4 val is that bills late in a Congress benefit from more accumulated same-Congress history. The notebook does not test this. The intervals are marginal, not paired, so they overstate the uncertainty of the gap.

D-c115-o3.interpretation: This is the calibration table behind D1. For each split it gives the chi-square of the standardized val-test gaps, the observed mean |relative gap| and the gap expected from noise alone. Observed and noise-expected relative gaps agree closely for S3 (0.037 vs 0.038, p = 0.54), S2 (0.039 vs 0.039, p = 0.63) and S3+stream (0.030 vs 0.034, p = 0.68). Only S1pool is rejected (0.120 vs 0.038, p = 0.012).
D-c115-o3.caveats: S1a+stream has a relative gap twice the noise level (0.074 vs 0.036) but passes at p = 0.096. With one fold the test cannot separate a real shift from chance.

D-c117-txt.interpretation: Across the 7 rolling test Congresses, Task 1 levels are stable. `sponsor_hist` and `rw2hop` both average 0.259 (CV about 0.03), and their between-fold std is about equal to the bootstrap SE (std/SE 0.93-1.00), so Congress-to-Congress movement is mostly sampling noise. Task 2 levels move: `eb_rate` std is 0.036 (std/SE 2.47) and `eb_rate_t0safe` std is 0.045 (std/SE 2.97). A single test Congress's Task 2 AUROC therefore mixes model quality with how hard that Congress is.
D-c117-txt.caveats: With 7 folds, the between-fold std is itself imprecise. The weak count baselines (`popularity`, std/SE 2.13) do show real level movement on Task 1.

D-c117-o0.interpretation: The four Task 1 baselines keep the same ordering in every test Congress from 112 to 118: popularity < party+pop < sponsor_hist ≈ rw2hop. The two history scores stay in a narrow 0.244-0.272 band. Congress 118 is the low point for every baseline (sponsor_hist 0.244, popularity 0.113), so the most recent Congress is somewhat harder, mainly for the popularity-type scores.
D-c117-o0.caveats: Test sizes grow from 3,230 bills (112) to 5,138-5,391 (116-118), so later points are estimated more precisely.

D-c117-o1.interpretation: Task 2 AUROC drifts. The policy-area model `eb_rate` falls from 0.78 (112) to about 0.69-0.70 (116-118). The at-introduction model and `chamber_maj` dip sharply in 116-117 (`eb_rate_t0safe` 0.569 and 0.560; `chamber_maj` 0.535 and 0.545) and partly recover in 118 (0.619). Because the dip shows up in the sponsor-majority signal, part of it is linked to which party controls which chamber. 116 and 117 both had a Democratic House.
D-c117-o1.caveats: The regime explanation is an inference. D26 finds that regime-matched training weights do not recover the loss for these count models, and the 95% bands in 116-118 are wide (about ±0.04).

D-c119-txt.interpretation: Validation picks good models from near-tie families. Task 1 regrets are tiny: `sponsor_hist` family mean 0.0028, `rw2hop` 0.0002, with Kendall tau 0.86-0.94 between val and test orderings. Val consistently picks the recency-weighted members (`sh_hl1` in 6/7 folds, `rw_b0.1_hl1` in 6/7). The Task 2 families have low hit rates (0.14-0.29) and low tau (0.24-0.43), because members differ by less than noise: the median val margin is 0.0005 AUROC. D12 passes with a mean regret of 0.0078 AUROC, above the 0.005 tolerance, because only 1 of 7 folds is significant; D12b (at-introduction family) passes with 0.0045. Selecting on the mean of the last three val folds (D17) cuts regrets further: 0.0015 for `eb_rate`, 0.0019 for `eb_rate_t0safe`. D5 (Task 1 main baselines keep their val-to-test order in only 57% of folds) is not a selection failure: it reflects the near-exact tie between `rw2hop` and `sponsor_hist` (paired mean difference -0.0002), whose order flips by chance; D6 (Task 2, candidates far apart) keeps its order in 100% of folds.
D-c119-txt.caveats: D12's pass rests on the two-part rule. Its mean regret exceeds tolerance and is driven by one fold (118). The 'test-best' is chosen on test, so regret is biased upward. That makes these passes conservative, but it also means the significance counts are liberal.

D-c119-o1.interpretation: Per-fold regret is zero or almost zero in most folds for every family. The exceptions: `sponsor_hist` at c=113 (0.014); the at-introduction Task 2 family at c=116-117 (0.013, 0.017); and above all `eb_rate` at c=118 (0.044 AUROC). The 116-117 values match the sign flip in the value of the sponsor-majority feature (dev-fold differences `eb_m20_t0s - eb_nomaj_m20_t0s` of -0.012 in 116 and +0.017 in 117). Validation on 116 favoured the variant without that feature, which then lost on 117.
D-c119-o1.caveats: The 0.044 regret at c=118 belongs to the policy-area `eb_rate` family: tuning that variant on the 117 validation Congress alone can cost several AUROC points on the locked test. The deployable at-introduction family has almost no regret at 118 (0.0001); its losses happen at 116-117 (0.013, 0.017). Both patterns support averaging selection over several val folds (D17).

D-c121-txt.interpretation: The learned embedding model behaves well under S3. Validation picks rank 256 or 512 with recency weighting in every fold. Regret is 0 in 4/7 folds and never significant (max 0.0032), and val-test level gaps are within noise (D22, D23 pass). The val-picked SVD is above the unweighted `sponsor_hist` reference on test in every fold, by +0.012 to +0.026 Recall@20 (mean 0.2801 vs 0.259). That comparison mixes two things, recency weighting and low-rank learning: every val pick is recency-weighted, and D26 shows that recency weighting alone adds +0.0209 to `sponsor_hist` (7/7 folds), which puts recency-weighted `sponsor_hist` at about 0.280 (0.259 + 0.021), essentially the SVD's level. The selection-transfer result (D22/D23) stands; the claim that a learned embedding beats count history does not.
D-c121-txt.caveats: The clean comparison would be `svd_hl1` vs `sh_hl1` on the same folds; the notebook does not print it, so the 0.280 figure for recency-weighted `sponsor_hist` is an additive estimate. The SVD has far fewer degrees of freedom than a GNN with message passing and learned feature transforms, so a pass here is necessary evidence, not sufficient evidence, that a GNN's validation choice will transfer. The picked rank sits at the top of the grid, so the optimum may lie beyond 512.

D-c121-o1.interpretation: Mean test Recall@20 rises steadily with SVD rank: from 0.241 (rank 8) to 0.280 (rank 512) with recency weighting, and from 0.194 to 0.260 without it. Recency weighting adds 0.02-0.05 at every rank. Recency-weighted ranks of 32 or more (0.263 and up) and unweighted rank 512 (0.2603) exceed the unweighted `sponsor_hist` reference (0.259). Lower rank (more compression) monotonically hurts, so higher capacity does not overfit across Congresses here. The two levers are capacity and weighting recent edges more; the top recency-weighted SVD (0.280) only matches what recency-weighted counts reach (about 0.280, see D26).
D-c121-o1.caveats: If gains keep rising up to rank 512, the model may simply be memorising pairwise history. Small GNN embeddings (32-128 dimensions) may need other inputs (features, multi-hop structure) to match it.

D-c122-txt.interpretation: 15.7% of positives (30,032) come from legislators with no training history. Both the SVD and `sponsor_hist` score zero on them: transductive cold start. Among returning legislators, the SVD's advantage over unweighted `sponsor_hist` stays positive when the member's role changed: +0.0167 after a majority-status flip (CI 0.014-0.019), +0.0233 after a committee-profile shift, versus +0.0197 for unchanged members. Members who switched chamber or party (only 1,440 positives, 0.75%) are poorly predicted by both models (about 0.07) with no difference between them. D25 passes: the difference-in-differences of 0.0029 gives no significant sign that the learned embeddings go stale.
D-c122-txt.caveats: The per-stratum advantages inherit the confound from D22/D23: the val-picked SVD is recency-weighted and `sponsor_hist` is not, so the levels mostly measure recency, not learning. The difference-in-differences cancels any recency effect that is equal across strata, but recency may help role-changed members differently, so D25 reads as 'no staleness detected for recency-weighted embeddings relative to unweighted counts'. 'Committee shift' is a proxy built from referral profiles, because committee rosters are not in the data. The chamber/party-switch stratum is too small to detect staleness.

D-c122-o1.interpretation: The bars make the cold-start gap clear. New legislators sit at essentially 0 recall for both models, while returning-unchanged members reach 0.26 (SVD) and 0.24 (`sponsor_hist`). Majority-flipped and committee-shift members fall in between (0.15-0.24; committee shift is lowest at 0.153 for `sponsor_hist` and 0.176 for the SVD). Chamber/party switchers are lowest among returning members (about 0.07).
D-c122-o1.caveats: Per-positive recall pools bills of different sizes, so it is not the same quantity as the per-bill Recall@20 used elsewhere.

D-c124-txt.interpretation: On the same test bills, the random split (S5) overstates Task 1 Recall@20 relative to the temporal split (S3): by +0.075 for `sponsor_hist` (0.334 vs 0.259) and +0.070 for `rw2hop`, significant in 7/7 Congresses. The inflation is smaller for `party+pop` (+0.021, 5/7) and `popularity` (+0.016, 4/7). It is largest for the models that exploit sponsor-specific history, the same signal a GNN would use. Task 2 `eb_rate` AUROC is 0.750 under the random split vs 0.724 under S3. The printed val margins (Task 1 0.0021, Task 2 0.0005) are far below the 0.01 MDE, so most near-tie choices are effectively ties.
D-c124-txt.caveats: The Task 2 gap of +0.026 is reported without a paired CI. The D7 verdict covers Task 1 only.

D-c124-o1.interpretation: In every test Congress the random-split score sits above the temporal one. The gap widens in recent Congresses: about +0.05 in 112 (0.325 vs 0.279) but +0.09 to +0.12 in 116-118 (for example 0.349 vs 0.226 in 118). A random split would therefore hide exactly the recent drift that matters for deploying on Congress 119.

D-c126-txt.interpretation: Same-Congress history is worth a lot for Task 1. The within-Congress split S4 beats S3 by +0.042 to +0.075 Recall@20 (mean 0.057). The leakage-free streaming protocol (S3+stream) beats plain S3 in every fold: +0.037 on average for `sponsor_hist` (range +0.026 to +0.053), +0.036 for `rw2hop`, +0.034 at t0=7. Streaming leaves Task 2 essentially unchanged (+0.001 AUROC). Under streaming, validation still predicts the Task 1 test level (D14 pass; mean |rel gap| 0.029 vs 0.040 plain). S4's Task 2 differences (+0.122, -0.007, +0.035) are erratic.
D-c126-txt.caveats: S4 mixes same-Congress history with a different bill population (the last 20% of bills, which tend to be late-session and possibly different in kind) and much smaller test sets. Streaming is the cleaner measure of the value of same-Congress history.

D-c126-o1.interpretation: The streaming line lies above the plain line in all 7 Congresses with no crossing, at about 0.29-0.31 vs 0.24-0.27. The gap is largest in 117-118 (+0.046, +0.053). Same-Congress history is therefore increasingly important in recent Congresses, which also makes the plain protocol increasingly pessimistic about a deployed temporal model.

D-c126-o3.interpretation: This is the calibration table behind D14. All three streaming splits pass, with S3+stream the best calibrated (chi-square 4.31 on 7 df, p = 0.74; observed relative gap 0.029 vs 0.034 expected from noise). Adding streaming history therefore does not make the validation Congress a worse proxy for test.
D-c126-o3.caveats: S1a+stream's observed gap (0.065) is almost twice the noise level (0.035), but one fold cannot reject it (p = 0.14).

D-c128-txt.interpretation: Paired sizing shows what each split can resolve. Large Task 1 differences are confirmed by any single test Congress: `sponsor_hist - party+pop` +0.058 and `svd - sponsor_hist` +0.021 (an unweighted reference, so this mostly reflects recency weighting), with p_miss_1C = 0. Smaller ones are not. The deployable Task 2 pair `eb_rate_t0safe - chamber_maj` (+0.020) goes unconfirmed in 43% of single Congresses, and the sponsor-majority near-tie (+0.083 on average) in 29%. So D9 fails for S1a, S1b, their streaming versions and S1pool, while S2 and S3 pass by averaging 7 folds. The protocol pairs are decisive: streaming +0.037 (never missed), and expanding minus sliding for unweighted `sponsor_hist` -0.012. D9b's deployment risk is large: the prediction half-width for the majority-feature effect in a new Congress is 15 times the MDE. Even a well-estimated average can be erased or reversed in Congress 119. D15 adds that a precise absolute Task 2 level would take about 13 test Congresses, against 1 for Task 1. The sponsor-cluster bootstrap CIs are 1.2-2.6 times wider than the naive bill-level ones (1.4-2.6 for S1b, S1pool and S3; 1.22 for the small S4 test sets).
D-c128-txt.caveats: The miss risk for k = 2 and k = 7 is a normal approximation for the *average* effect, while the k = 1 value is empirical and includes Congress-to-Congress heterogeneity. They are different quantities, and multi-fold splits pass more easily by construction. The SD estimates use 7 dependent folds.

D-c128-o1.interpretation: For each relevant pair, the chart compares the miss risk with one test Congress, the mean of 2 and the mean of 7. All Task 1 model pairs are at or near 0 everywhere. Above the 20% line (80% power): the two Task 2 pairs with one Congress (`eb_rate_t0safe - chamber_maj` 0.43, sponsor-majority near-tie 0.29) and with two (0.32, 0.47), and `sh_hl1 - sh_none+caucus` with two (0.41; it is 0.14 with one). With 7 Congresses these drop to 0.005-0.033.
D-c128-o1.caveats: The k = 1 values are empirical shares and include Congress-to-Congress heterogeneity, while the k = 2 and k = 7 values are normal approximations for the *average* effect. They are not directly comparable: the k = 2 risk can exceed the k = 1 risk (majority pair 0.47 vs 0.29; `sh_hl1` pair 0.41 vs 0.14), which is a difference of method, not evidence that pooling hurts. Most of the gain from k = 7 reflects a narrower target (the average effect), not more certainty about any particular future Congress. Compare D9b.

D-c130-txt.interpretation: Without recency weighting, the expanding window loses to a 3-Congress sliding window. The paired differences are -0.012 (`sponsor_hist`), -0.012 (`rw2hop`) and -0.020 (`popularity`) Recall@20, with the sliding window significantly better in 6/7 folds. With recency weighting (half-life 1 Congress) the gap disappears: -0.0008 for `sh_hl1`, -0.0007 for `rw_b0.3_hl1`, -0.0003 for the val-picked SVD, each significant in at most 1 fold. For Task 2 the expanding window is marginally better (+0.0027 AUROC). D10 passes. Old Congresses are not harmful in themselves; what hurts is weighting them equally with recent ones.
D-c130-txt.caveats: Folds share most training data, so the '6/7 folds' count is descriptive. Only k = 3 was tested as the sliding window.

D-c130-o1.interpretation: The unweighted `sponsor_hist` line sits below zero in every fold (down to -0.018 in 115). The recency-weighted and SVD lines hug zero (within ±0.003). Task 2 is mostly slightly positive (up to +0.011 in 114). Recency weighting makes the choice of window irrelevant, so the expanding window can be kept as long as recent edges get more weight.

D-c132-txt.interpretation: Upweighting training Congresses whose House/Senate majorities match the target Congress (x2) does not help once recency weighting is used. Regime+recency minus recency is +0.0011 Recall@20 for Task 1 (better in 1 fold, worse in 0) and -0.0001 AUROC for Task 2. Regime weighting alone is clearly worse than recency alone for Task 1 (-0.016, worse in 5/7 folds), while recency over unweighted helps in 7/7 folds (+0.021). D26 passes: recency weighting is sufficient for these count baselines, and regime upweighting adds nothing on top. It does not fix the Task 2 level drift: recency adds only +0.0096 AUROC to `eb_rate_t0safe` (significant in 2/7 folds), and D2b still fails.
D-c132-txt.caveats: Only 5 of 7 folds have a regime-matched training Congress. Only a x2 weight and count/rate models were tested. A GNN with explicit majority-status features could use regime information differently.

D-c132-o1.interpretation: The per-fold differences are all tiny (|diff| <= 0.0075, the largest being Task 1 at c=113) and scattered around zero. Folds 112 and 116 are exactly zero because no training Congress shared their regime. Nothing here points to a systematic regime benefit.

D-c134-txt.interpretation: Hiding the policy area when it would not yet be assigned at introduction costs `eb_rate` 0.05-0.15 AUROC per Congress (mean 0.10). The largest drops are in 112 (0.155) and 116-117 (0.119, 0.133). Measured as discrimination above chance, `eb_rate` has 0.724 - 0.5 = 0.224 and `eb_rate_t0safe` keeps 0.624 - 0.5 = 0.124, so about 45% of `eb_rate`'s signal (0.10 of 0.22) depends on the policy area, ranging from about 24% (114) to 69% (117) per Congress. This counts as leakage only if Task 2 is scored at introduction, which the notebook adopts as an assumption; the task definition (reported within 180 days) does not fix the prediction time. Under that assumption a policy-area feature would leak future information under every split.
D-c134-txt.caveats: The share of bills without a policy area comes from 56 recent bills and is applied uniformly. A model that predicts the policy area from bill text would recover some of the gap.

D-c136-txt.interpretation: Switching from the legacy pool (everyone who served that Congress) to the point-in-time pool raises Recall@20 by only about +0.002 for all baselines, and their ordering does not change. The candidate-pool definition is not a material source of evaluation bias.

D-c138-txt.interpretation: With hyperparameters fixed from validation, refitting on train+val (adding Congress c-1) raises Task 1 test Recall@20 substantially in 7/7 folds: +0.059 (`sponsor_hist`), +0.065 (`rw2hop`), +0.064 (SVD). The gain is smaller under streaming (+0.024 to +0.026), because same-Congress history partly substitutes for c-1. Task 2 gains a little (+0.005 AUROC, 3 folds better, 0 worse). The immediately preceding Congress is the most informative history for Task 1. D19 passes.
D-c138-txt.caveats: For a GNN the analogous step is a refit with a fixed epoch budget, or at least adding c-1's edges to the message-passing graph at test time. The SVD and count models, which have no training dynamics, cannot show whether a fixed budget transfers.

D-c138-o1.interpretation: In every fold the three Task 1 refit-gain series cluster at about +0.045 to +0.076, far above zero. The Task 2 series stays near zero (-0.0004 to +0.012). Refitting is clearly worthwhile for cosponsor prediction and harmless for advancement.

D-c140-txt.interpretation: Reserving 118 as a locked test costs little overall, with one Task 2 exception. Every selection check still passes on the 6 development folds 112-117. Task 1 regrets stay small, and the policy-area `eb_rate` regret drops from 0.0078 to 0.0017 once fold 118 is left out. But the deployable at-introduction family `eb_rate_t0safe` (the one D12b judges) rises from 0.0045 to 0.0053, above the 0.005 tolerance; it passes only because no fold is individually significant, and with hit rate 0.29 and tau 0.24 validation is weak at choosing among t0-safe variants. The maximum paired miss risk rises from 0.033 to 0.115, under the 0.20 bar, and the median CI half-width of mean differences grows only from 0.0076 to 0.0080. The development folds predict 118 reasonably well: 8 of 9 relevant paired differences fall inside the development prediction interval. `sponsor_hist`'s absolute level on 118 (0.2439) falls just below its interval (mean 0.2617 ± 0.0172), so 118 is marginally harder than the development Congresses. implications: Use the rolling-origin by-Congress split (S3) as the backbone: train 108..c-2, validate on c-1, refit on 108..c-1, test on c. Develop on folds 112-117, score locked Congress 118 once at the end, and treat 119 as prospective. Do not use a single test Congress (S1a/S1b) or pooled 117+118 to compare models: one Congress misses a real +0.02 AUROC Task 2 difference 43% of the time. Select Task 2 hyperparameters on the mean over several validation Congresses (D17: at-introduction regret 0.0019), not on c-1 alone: on the dev folds the c-1 rule's regret is 0.0053, above tolerance.

Evaluate the temporal GNN in streaming mode. Include the eval Congress's cosponsorship edges dated on or before introduced_date + t0 in the message-passing graph. This is leakage-free, matches deployment, and is worth about +0.037 Recall@20 for simple history models in every fold. Whether it also helps the 15.7% of positives from new members is a hypothesis to test (D24 strata under S3+stream); it was not measured, and `popularity` gains only +0.0035 from streaming.

Encode time or weight recent edges (recency half-life of about 1 Congress, or a time encoding or decay in the temporal GNN). Then keep the expanding window: unweighted history loses about 0.012 Recall@20 to a 3-Congress window, and weighted history does not. Regime-matched upweighting adds nothing beyond recency for these baselines. Compare the GNN against recency-weighted `sponsor_hist` (about 0.280), not the unweighted 0.259: the SVD's apparent +0.021 'learning' gain is roughly matched by recency weighting alone (additive estimate 0.259 + 0.021; the direct `svd_hl1` vs `sh_hl1` comparison was not run).

After choosing hyperparameters and the epoch budget on validation (c-1 for Task 1, the mean of several validation Congresses for Task 2), refit on train+val, or at minimum add Congress c-1's edges to the graph at test time. Leaving out the most recent Congress costs about 0.06 Recall@20.

For Task 2, fix the prediction time explicitly and build features as of that time. The policy area is usually missing at introduction and inflates AUROC by about 0.10 (about 45% of `eb_rate`'s signal above chance). Report the at-introduction model as the primary result and policy-area models as a 'one month after introduction' variant.

Report Task 1 as per-fold scores plus the 7-fold mean, and Task 2 levels per Congress with their spread, never as one number (between-Congress std about 0.04 AUROC). Use sponsor-cluster bootstrap CIs (1.2-2.6 times wider than bill-level) and paired CIs for model comparisons.

Treat the random split only as a leaky upper bound. It inflates Recall@20 by +0.075 (about 29%), most strongly for the sponsor-history signal a GNN relies on. Give the GNN inductive node features (party/caucus, chamber, state, committee proxies) so it can handle new legislators that a pure embedding model cannot.
open_questions: Will a GNN's validation choices (epochs, depth, embedding size) transfer as well as the SVD's? The SVD has no training dynamics, so D22/D23 are only a lower bar for a model with message passing and early stopping. Does any learned model beat recency-weighted counts at all? The notebook never runs `svd_hl1` vs `sh_hl1` directly.

How much of the Task 2 drop in 116-117 is regime-driven? The value of the sponsor-majority feature flips sign there, and its prediction interval for a new Congress is 15 times the MDE. Count-based regime weighting does not fix it, so whether a GNN with majority-status features can is untested.

Is Congress 118 representative of 119? 118 is marginally harder than the development folds for `sponsor_hist`, and the Task 2 at-introduction advantage almost vanishes there. One locked Congress cannot separate a real trend from noise.
The at-introduction policy-area missingness (86%) comes from 56 bills of an unfinished Congress. Historical CRS lag may differ, which would change the size of the Task 2 leakage correction.
